original_question: Determine under what conditions the nonlocal models from Section 2.2.2 admit solutions under homogeneous Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions when the perceptual kernel is explicitly truncated near the boundary, and compare those results against the periodic case.
target_in_paper: Open Problem 39 in §4.1.2 (Boundary conditions): the paper asks, for the problems introduced in §2.2.2, when solutions exist under homogeneous Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions when the perceptual kernel is defined in the boundary-truncated style of (4.3), and how those results compare with the periodic-boundary case. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s actual target. It correctly identifies the §2.2.2 dynamic-memory/nonlocal-perception setting, asks an existence question under homogeneous Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions, singles out the explicitly boundary-truncated perceptual kernel rather than the periodic spill-over convention, and asks for comparison with the periodic case. Those are exactly the distinctive features of Open Problem 39. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
missing_details: The paper’s formulation is not about arbitrary nonlocal PDEs, but about the §2.2.2 dynamic-memory problems, i.e. the class of models in which perception enters through a spatially nonlocal perceived potential a_g,R built from a perceptual kernel g and radius R. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

To be paper-faithful, the question should say that the kernel is defined 'in the style of (4.3)': in one dimension on a bounded interval (0,L), the top-hat averaging window is cut off near x=0 and x=L and renormalized by the available window length, with 0 < R < L. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The draft should specify bounded-domain geometry, since the boundary issue only arises there; the periodic comparison is precisely the bounded-domain periodic case, where the kernel is treated by periodic spill-over. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The surrounding discussion distinguishes homogeneous Neumann from zero-flux: Neumann need not conserve total population unless the potential also satisfies the compatible normal-derivative condition. That hidden boundary-condition subtlety is part of the context of Open Problem 39. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

If the question is to be fully stand-alone, it should clarify that Open Problem 39 is a synthesis of the earlier §2.2.2 existence questions posed for particular models and boundary settings (notably Open Problems 5, 9, 11, and 20, together with their periodic analogues). ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The paper does not ask here for uniqueness, regularity class, or long-time asymptotics; the sharp paper-faithful target is existence of solutions and comparison with the periodic case, not a stronger well-posedness theorem. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

For context, the paper notes that existence theory is only partially available for smoother kernels (e.g. twice continuously differentiable kernels for model (2.10)), while the top-hat kernel is the analytically hardest case; this explains why the cutoff-top-hat formulation should be named explicitly. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

The algebraic template items mentioned in your instructions (ambient ring/field, homogeneity degree, nilpotency, 'sufficiently large m') are not applicable here; the relevant hidden data are instead the spatial domain, time dependence vs. steady state, the perceived-potential operator, the perceptual radius, and the precise boundary conditions. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
refined_question: For the dynamic-memory advection–diffusion and advection–diffusion–reaction problems introduced in §2.2.2, in which nonlocality enters through a perceived potential of the form a_g,R(x,t)=∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy, work on a bounded domain and replace the periodic 'spill-over' interpretation of the top-hat perceptual kernel by the boundary-truncated, renormalized operator used in (4.3) (in one dimension, T_R[a](x,t)=|((x-R,x+R)∩(0,L))|^{-1}∫_{(x-R,x+R)∩(0,L)} a(y,t)dy). Under what hypotheses do solutions exist when homogeneous Neumann or homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed, and how do the resulting existence results compare with those in the corresponding periodic-boundary setting? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
justification: The nearest official target is Open Problem 39, not the broader neighboring Open Problem 40. Open Problem 39 matches every distinctive element in the draft: it explicitly references the §2.2.2 problems, homogeneous Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions, the kernel 'defined in the style of (4.3)', and comparison with the periodic case. Open Problem 40 is broader and asks for alternative kernel constructions near the boundary; your draft does not ask for new constructions, only for existence under the specific cutoff construction. The nearby boundary-condition discussion explains why periodic problems are easier (the kernel spills over the boundary on the torus) and why the truncated kernel is biologically reasonable, while §5.1.1 explains why the higher-order nonlinearity and especially the top-hat kernel make existence difficult. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))
